questions.stem: Two identical light bulbs B1 and B2 are connected in series with a 6 V battery. A student claims that Bulb B1 glows brighter than Bulb B2 because Bulb B1 consumes electric current first, leaving less current for B2. Explain using physical conservation laws whether this statement is correct.

options.text: The statement is correct because electric current is consumed sequentially by loads in a circuit.
The statement is incorrect because electric charge is strictly conserved (I = dQ/dt is identical everywhere in a single series loop); both bulbs glow with equal brightness.
The statement is correct only if the battery is connected backwards.

questions.authoritative_solution: In a series circuit, there is only one continuous conducting pathway. By conservation of charge, the rate of charge flow (current I) entering any component equals the current leaving it. Energy is transferred, but charge is never consumed or destroyed. Hence, current is identical at all points, and both identical bulbs glow with identical brightness.
sample_misconception_responses: Current gets used up by Bulb 1 so Bulb 2 gets less current and glows dimmer.
Bulb 1 consumes some amperes so B2 has fewer amps left.
sample_correct_responses: Charge is strictly conserved in a closed loop, so current is identical through both series bulbs; neither bulb consumes current.
sample_slip_responses: Bulb 1 gets twice the voltage but same current.

questions.stem: A 12 V battery is connected to a 6-ohm resistor R1. A second resistor R2 of 3 ohms is then connected in parallel across R1. What happens to the total current drawn from the 12 V battery?

options.text: Total current remains constant at 2 A because batteries supply a fixed, invariant current rating.
Total current decreases to 1.33 A because adding another resistor increases overall resistance to 9 ohms.
Total current increases from 2 A to 6 A because adding a parallel branch reduces the equivalent circuit resistance to 2 ohms.

questions.authoritative_solution: A battery maintains a constant terminal potential difference (12 V), not constant current. In parallel: 1/Req = 1/6 + 1/3 = 3/6 => Req = 2 ohms. Total current I = V / Req = 12 / 2 = 6 A (Branch 1 draws 2 A, Branch 2 draws 4 A; total 6 A).
sample_misconception_responses: Batteries supply constant current so total amps stay 2 A.
sample_correct_responses: Adding a parallel branch decreases equivalent resistance to 2 ohms, so current increases to 6 A.
sample_slip_responses: Current decreases to 1.33 A because 6+3=9 ohms.

questions.stem: Two electric bulbs are rated 220 V, 100 W and 220 V, 40 W respectively. Calculate the ratio of their operating resistances (R_100 / R_40).

options.text: R_100 / R_40 = 2.5 (believing power is directly proportional to resistance in all appliances)
R_100 / R_40 = 1.0 (believing both bulbs have identical resistance)

questions.authoritative_solution: Power P = V^2 / R => R = V^2 / P at rated voltage. For Bulb 1: R_100 = 220^2 / 100 = 484 ohms. For Bulb 2: R_40 = 220^2 / 40 = 1210 ohms. Ratio R_100 / R_40 = 40 / 100 = 0.4 (or 2/5). The higher wattage bulb has lower filament resistance.
sample_misconception_responses: Formula: P = I^2 * R | Given: P1 = 100, P2 = 40 | Working: R1/R2 = 100/40 = 2.5 | Unit: Ω
sample_correct_responses: Formula: R = V^2 / P | Given: V = 220 V, P1 = 100 W, P2 = 40 W | Working: R1/R2 = P2/P1 = 40/100 = 0.4 | Unit: Ω
sample_slip_responses: Formula: R = V/P | Given: V=220, P=100 | Working: R1 = 2.2, R2 = 5.5 => 0.4 | Unit: Ω

questions.stem: A cylindrical metal wire of length L and cross-sectional area A has electrical resistance R. If the wire is stretched uniformly to double its original length (2L), what is its new resistance?

options.text: 2R (doubling length simply doubles resistance without affecting area)
4R (because volume is conserved: when length doubles, area halves to A/2)
R / 2 (resistance decreases when wire becomes longer)

questions.authoritative_solution: Volume of the wire is conserved during stretching: V = A * L = A_new * (2L) => A_new = A / 2. New resistance R_new = rho * (2L) / (A / 2) = 4 * (rho * L / A) = 4R.
sample_misconception_responses: New resistance is 2R because R is proportional to length.
sample_correct_responses: When wire is stretched to 2L, area becomes A/2 by volume conservation, making resistance 4R.

questions.stem: Two resistors R1 = 6 Ω and R2 = 3 Ω are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery. Calculate the total circuit current (I) supplied by the battery.

options.text: I = 1.33 A (using R_total = 6 + 3 = 9 Ω by mistake)
I = 6.0 A (equivalent resistance R_eq = 2 Ω; I = 12 / 2)
I = 4.0 A (only calculating current in one branch)

questions.authoritative_solution: For parallel combination: 1/Req = 1/6 + 1/3 = 3/6 = 1/2 => Req = 2 Ω. Total current I = V / Req = 12 V / 2 Ω = 6 A.
sample_misconception_responses: Formula: I = V / (R1 + R2) | Given: R1 = 6, R2 = 3, V = 12 | Working: Req = 9 Ω => I = 12/9 = 1.33 | Unit: A
sample_correct_responses: Formula: 1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2, I = V / Req | Given: R1 = 6, R2 = 3, V = 12 | Working: 1/Req = 1/2 => Req = 2 Ω, I = 12/2 = 6 | Unit: A
sample_slip_responses: Formula: I = V * Req | Given: V = 12, Req = 2 | Working: I = 24 | Unit: A

questions.stem: In an electrical circuit experiment, an ammeter is always connected in series with the component, whereas a voltmeter is always connected in parallel. Explain why connecting an ammeter in parallel could damage the circuit.

options.text: An ammeter has extremely low internal resistance; connecting it in parallel creates a short circuit, drawing dangerously large current that burns the meter.
An ammeter has infinite internal resistance and would block all battery current.
An ammeter reverses the battery polarity when placed in parallel.

questions.authoritative_solution: An ammeter is designed with nearly zero internal resistance so it does not alter current when placed in series. If connected in parallel across a voltage source, its negligible resistance causes a massive short-circuit current (I = V/R -> very high), potentially destroying the meter.
sample_misconception_responses: An ammeter has infinite resistance and halts current.
sample_correct_responses: An ammeter has near-zero internal resistance. Connecting it in parallel creates a short circuit drawing excessive current that can burn the meter.
sample_slip_responses: An ammeter cannot be used in parallel because voltage equals current.

questions.stem: An electric heater has a resistance of 10 Ω and carries a steady current of 2 A. Calculate the amount of thermal heat energy (H) produced by the heater in 30 seconds.

options.text: H = 600 J (using H = I * R * t instead of I^2)
H = 1200 J (using Joule Law: H = I^2 * R * t = 4 * 10 * 30)
H = 200 J (forgetting time factor in formula)

questions.authoritative_solution: By Joules Law of Heating: H = I^2 * R * t. Substituting I = 2 A, R = 10 ohms, t = 30 s: H = 2^2 * 10 * 30 = 4 * 10 * 30 = 1200 Joules.
sample_misconception_responses: Formula: H = I * R * t | Given: I = 2, R = 10, t = 30 | Working: H = 2 * 10 * 30 = 600 | Unit: J
sample_correct_responses: Formula: H = I^2 * R * t | Given: I = 2 A, R = 10 Ω, t = 30 s | Working: H = 4 * 10 * 30 = 1200 | Unit: J
sample_slip_responses: Formula: H = V * I | Given: I = 2, R = 10 | Working: H = 200 | Unit: J

questions.stem: How much work (W) is done in moving a charge of 2 Coulombs across two points in a circuit having a potential difference of 12 Volts?

options.text: 6 Joules (dividing V by Q: 12 / 2)
24 Joules (using W = V * Q = 12 * 2)
14 Joules (adding voltage and charge: 12 + 2)

questions.authoritative_solution: Potential difference V is the work done per unit charge: V = W / Q => W = V * Q = 12 V * 2 C = 24 Joules.
sample_correct_responses: Work done W = V * Q = 12 * 2 = 24 Joules.

questions.stem: Explain two major practical reasons why electrical appliances in household domestic circuits are connected in parallel with each other, rather than in series.

options.text: In parallel, each appliance operates at full 220 V and can be turned on/off independently without breaking the entire circuit; in series, if one appliance fails, all stop.
Connecting in parallel increases overall resistance so electric bills are cut in half.
In series circuits, alternating current converts into direct current spontaneously.

questions.authoritative_solution: In parallel connection: (1) Each appliance receives full supply voltage (220 V) ensuring rated power output. (2) Each appliance has its own independent switch; if one device fails or is turned off, other branches continue operating. In series, total resistance would be enormous and any open-circuit stops all devices.
sample_misconception_responses: Parallel connections increase resistance to reduce electricity bills.
sample_correct_responses: Parallel circuits provide identical rated 220 V across each appliance and allow independent switching so failure of one does not interrupt others.

questions.stem: An electric fuse is a critical safety device installed in household circuits. What are the key physical properties of a fuse wire, and how does it protect appliances?

options.text: Made of an alloy with low melting point; excessive current produces Joule heat that melts the fuse, breaking the circuit before appliances overheat.
Made of thick copper with high melting point so it never melts under large currents.
Acts as a magnetic switch that repels excess electrons back into the substation.

questions.authoritative_solution: A fuse is connected in series in the live wire. It consists of a lead-tin alloy having suitable resistance and low melting point. When current exceeds safe rating (short-circuit/overload), Joule heating (H = I^2*R*t) melts the wire, opening the circuit safely.
sample_misconception_responses: Fuse is made of thick copper with high melting point to conduct all power.
sample_correct_responses: A fuse has a low melting point so excessive current causes it to melt and break the circuit safely.
sample_slip_responses: Fuse acts as a voltage transformer.
